title: Corpus Christi
hook: Catholics carry the sacrament through the streets in procession

segments.voice: Yesterday, Trinity Sunday: the sea that won't fit in a hole in the sand. Your line was three in one. What did you let stay bigger than you? Day one thousand forty-three, and the end of a week.

A small bell rings at the corner, and the street goes quiet. Down the middle of the road, over a carpet of flower petals someone spent all night laying out, comes a procession: children in white, a band, people carrying candles, and under a canopy held up on poles, a priest holding something gold and shining in both hands. In its center is a small round wafer of bread. As it passes, people on the sidewalk kneel. A man stops on his bike and takes off his cap. A shopkeeper steps out of her doorway to watch. This happens in some Catholic towns and parishes on one feast, and the feast's name is just two Latin words. Today, Corpus Christi.
screen: `A BELL, AND THE STREET GOES QUIET.`

segments.voice: Corpus Christi is Latin for the body of Christ. The words go back to the night before Jesus died. Paul passes them on in a letter, in the King James Bible: Jesus took bread, gave thanks, broke it, and said, "this is my body, which is broken for you: this do in remembrance of me." In John's Gospel Jesus says, "I am the living bread which came down from heaven." Christians have understood those words in more than one way. Catholic teaching holds that at Mass the bread truly becomes the body of Christ, and that he remains present in it afterward. So the consecrated host can be kept, honored and carried, and on this feast it's taken out of the church and through the streets. Orthodox Christians also speak of the bread truly becoming Christ's body, though this procession belongs to the Western calendar, and some Anglican churches mark the day too. Other Protestants understand communion as a remembrance, or as Christ present by the Spirit to those who receive it, and wouldn't carry the bread in procession. Each takes the words seriously. They hear them differently. Here's what the procession itself says, for those who keep it. What happens at the altar isn't meant to stay behind the church doors. It goes past the bakery, the bus stop, the apartments with laundry on the balconies. That fits the week we've just walked. Two friends on the road to Emmaus, who knew him in the breaking of bread. A parish walking its boundaries. A crowd in the street hearing the news in their own languages. Again and again this week, the holy went outside.

Here's the practice: walk your streets in your mind, one stop at a time, the way a procession pauses. Settle, and breathe. This time, don't start from your own door. Start with the busiest place you pass in an ordinary week: a station, a supermarket line, a school gate. Bring the crowd there to mind, the faces you half know. Then a quieter place: a bench, a laundromat, a clinic waiting room. Then the place you'll be tonight. If you pray, you can pray for the people in each place, the way the procession blesses the streets it moves through. If you don't, simply hold each place as if it mattered, because to someone it does. The bell holds the time.
Corpus Christi. Latin for the body of Christ: a feast when Catholics carry the consecrated bread out of the church and through the streets.
Your line: christ in the streets. Today, treat one ordinary street you walk as if something holy might come down it, and greet one person on it. Day one thousand forty-three, the end of a week.

notes: Week end (day 1043): the teach looks back at the week's walking days (Emmaus, Rogation bounds, Pentecost street crowd).

Range of eucharistic views (Catholic real presence and reservation; Orthodox; Anglican and Lutheran observance; Protestant memorial or spiritual presence) is compressed; confirm fair to each, especially 'some Anglican churches mark the day too'.

Protestant views are given as 'other Protestants' after naming Anglican observance; Lutheran teaching on real presence is not covered by 'other Protestants' (remembrance / spiritual presence); confirm.
The hook (petal carpets, canopy, kneeling) is illustrative and attributed to 'some Catholic towns and parishes'; no date of the feast's founding is given.

Editor pass: 'one day a year' (an unsourced count) became 'one feast'; the practice no longer repeats 1039's (a mental walk from your front door to the corner, praying at each stretch) and now moves through three kinds of places, busy, quiet and tonight's. Quotations verified against KJV.
Second editor pass: 'Catholics believe' (a claim about every Catholic) became 'Catholic teaching holds'.

Audit pass: cut 'Lutheran' from churches that mark Corpus Christi (Luther and the Lutheran confessions rejected the feast and its procession; observance is rare).
